prospects.thesis: HII is America's largest military shipbuilder with a near-monopoly on nuclear-powered carriers and submarines, benefiting from accelerated Navy fleet expansion and the AUKUS submarine pact. At 0.9x P/S with +6.5% 1M momentum and bullish institutional/options flow, it trades at a meaningful discount to defense peers despite a record backlog. With VIX elevated at 28, defense names offer defensive beta plus secular tailwinds from the FY27 defense budget cycle.

RTX offers diversified exposure across Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney, and Raytheon missile systems, with the Patriot and LTAMDS air defense franchises seeing surging global demand. The GTF engine issue is largely in the rearview, freeing cash flow for buybacks, while bullish options and institutional positioning confirm smart-money accumulation. Large-cap stability is attractive with VIX at 28.

Qualcomm is the only non-defense pick among top-scored names and provides essential diversification, with its Snapdragon platform expanding into automotive (QCT Auto growing 40%+) and on-device AI PC/edge inference via Snapdragon X Elite. The -6.1% 1M pullback creates a better entry point while options flow has turned bullish ahead of the next product cycle. P/S of 4.2x remains reasonable for a tier-1 semi.

Booz Allen provides differentiated exposure to defense IT/AI consulting, distinct from the hardware primes, with heavy involvement in DoD AI implementation, cyber, and intelligence community modernization. Strong +6.2% 1M momentum and bullish options confirm institutional interest despite the bearish institutional read, and its 0.9x P/S is attractive for a services business with recurring government revenue. Catalyst: FY27 budget AI/cyber line items.

LMT's -5.7% 1M pullback on F-35 program noise creates a contrarian setup in a name with the world's largest missile/munitions backlog (THAAD, PAC-3, Javelin, HIMARS) amid depleted Western inventories. Bullish options and institutional flow suggest smart money is buying the dip, and the 1.7x P/S is below historical averages. Wait for stabilization before committing.

Meanwhile, the smart money is quietly heading for the exits in Consumer Staples, Consumer Discretionary, and Financials — the Staples hedging is the weird one because that's supposed to be the "safe" sector, which tells me institutions are worried about tariff-driven margin squeeze on companies that import goods and can't fully pass costs to a stretched consumer. Financials getting hedged likely reflects nervousness about regional bank commercial real estate exposure and whatever the current administration does with bank capital rules, while Healthcare bearishness smells like drug pricing pressure and ongoing Medicare negotiation headlines nobody wants to be long into. The pattern over the next month or two usually means a defensive rotation into rate-sensitive and hard-asset plays while people brace for a consumer slowdown — not a crash setup, more of a "growth is cooling" setup.
